..
Monday-Tuesday: Zonal or westerly flow will reside over the PacNW
to start the work week. This will have several impacts to the 
weather across the Inland NW. First off will be persistent onshore
flow piling cooler marine air west of the Cascade Crest and 
producing a persistent west to east pressure gradient across the 
Inland NW. This will result in breezy winds across the open wheat 
country of the Palouse, Columbia Basin, Snake River Valley, and 
West Plains. Wind gusts of 15 to 20 mph will be common. Winds will
be enhanced through the Cascade Gaps and river valleys, 
especially in the late afternoon and evening when the diurnal 
flows align. Probabilities via the NBM/HREF range anywhere from 30
to 60% for wind gusts in excess of 30 mph for locations like 
Wenatchee, Entiat, Waterville, Winthrop, and Malott. This will 
undoubtedly lead to elevated fire weather conditions with a few 
hours in the early evening flirting with critical thresholds, 
especially around the Waterville Plateau and Western Basin. 
Elevated humidity levels are the one driving factor for messaging 
this as elevated vs critical and with the push we are observing 
this evening, humidities are between 30-45% which should be the 
case each evening. Winds are also being enhanced by embedded waves
and cool fronts. One is traversing the area tonight and another 
will be arriving Tuesday evening/night. The lack of amplification 
to the midlevel flow will result in more seasonal temperatures 
which will be capped further by areas of dense smoke. Speaking of 
smoke, this will remain an tremendous impact across the region 
with air quality generally in the unhealthy to very unhealthy 
across the north and unhealthy to moderate south.

Wednesday-Thursday: High pressure amplifies over the Gulf of AK 
allowing an upper-level trough to carve into the Northwest. An 
axis of moisture strung across the Northern Rockies will get 
pulled into the trough while lapse rates increase under a -15C 
500mb cold pool. Surface based CAPE increases between 200-500 J/kg
across northern WA and North Idaho on Wednesday afternoon 
resulting in a 10-40% chance for developing showers and 
thunderstorms. The greatest threat (~ 40%) will be closer to the 
International border but 10-30% chances reside as far south as the
Highway 2 corridor from the Cascades to the Idaho Panhandle. 
Effective shear will be not be supportive of organized updrafts 
with forecast values on the order of 20-25 kts suggesting short-
lived cells but given the projected CAPE and drier sub-cloud 
layers coupled with downward capes (DCAPE) of 600-1100 J/kg, would
expect any sort of rain cooled air to produce erratic outflow 
winds of 20 to 30 mph. Not only will this be a concern for 
firefighters, but these small scale boundaries could provide a 
source of lift for new cells to develop, especially where NBM 
probabilities are closer to 10%. On another note, confidence is 
moderate to high for a higher concentration of convective cells to
develop in southern BC, this will need to be monitored for a more
robust outflow boundary coming in from the north and northeast. 
The threat for showers will linger into the early night across the
northern counties and would expect another day of hit or miss 
showers and weak thunderstorms to develop again Thursday though 
the highest probabilities for thunderstorms will migrate into far 
Northeastern WA and North Idaho as the 500mb cold pool begins to 
drift to the northeast while upper level temperatures over Central
WA warm 1 to 2 Celsius. 

Friday-Sunday: The general consensus of the ensembles for late week 
into the weekend is for another shift in the upper-level pattern 
toward a more dominant trough over the Eastern Pacific and 
amplifying ridge over the Northern Rockies. This eventually places
the Inland NW under southwest flow aloft. This pattern would be 
supportive of a subtle warming trend along with an increasing 
trend toward unsettled weather. The details are still fuzzy but 
there remains moderate confidence for this large scale synoptic 
pattern to set up over time. Most likely scenario is for showers 
and thunderstorm chances to be highest around the Blue Mountains 
and Camas Prairie as modified monsoonal moisture makes the north 
and northeastward track but as the air mass warms and moistens 
slowly, would not rule out surface based convection over any of 
the mountains, especially if any smaller disturbances eject from 
the offshore trough and rippled through the southwest flow. /sb
